newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. sends envoy to defuse Israel-PLO crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sends envoy to defuse Israel-PLO crisis.

text.p: The United States sent its Middle East envoy back to the region for talks on Thursday with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and later with Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu to try to defuse a growing crisis.

"I am concerned about it. I think everybody in the world who has worked for peace in the Middle East is concerned about it. We're all going to put our heads together and do the best we can," U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday.

A State Department spokesman said envoy Dennis Ross was carrying messages to both men from Clinton, who told reporters Washington would try to stop Israeli-Palestinian violence and restart peace talks.
Israel said Ross must press the Palestinian Authority to crack down on militant Moslem groups in the wake of a Tel Aviv suicide bombing that killed three Israeli women on Friday.

"We expect and we would like to see the Palestinian Authority fight terrorism. This is the first order of the day if we are going to salvage the peace process," Netanyahu said in a speech in central Israel.

Palestinian officials called on Ross to lean on Israel to halt work on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, where groundbreaking last week touched off seven straight days of clashes in the West Bank that show no signs of abating.

"We hope that Mr Ross will be speaking loudly and clearly to Mr Netanyahu to stop the causes that led to violence -- to stop his bulldozers, to stop his settlements and to put the peace process back on track," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said.

Ross stopped in Morocco on Wednesday night to see Arafat, who was on his way there after a visit to Bangladesh. Foreign ministers from the 16-member Al-Qods (Jerusalem) committee will also meet in Morocco on Thursday.
Ross will fly on to Israel then return home at the weekend to brief Clinton. Netanyahu's office said the prime minister would meet Ross in Jerusalem late on Thursday or on Friday.

Violence between Palestinians and Israeli troops flared again on Wednesday, this time in self-ruled Ramallah in the West Bank where hundreds of Arabs threw stones and bottles to challenge soldiers at a checkpoint.
Troops responded with rubber bullets and tear gas. A Ramallah hospital said about 25 protesters were treated for rubber bullet wounds or tear gas inhalation.

Israeli political analysts said Ross faced a tall order as he did last year when -- after a wave of violence claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis -- he brokered Israel's hand-over of most of Hebron to self-rule.

Israel Television reported the envoy would propose a compromise whereby the Palestinian Authority would clamp down on hard-line Islamic groups in return for an Israeli commitment not to make any more unilateral moves relating to the peace process.
Palestinians were enraged by Israel's recent decision to limit to nine percent the amount of West Bank territory to be handed over in the first of three troop re-deployments from mostly rural areas.
The Authority wanted three times as much territory and a say in determining the scope of the pullbacks.

Asked what influence Ross would have on the two sides, Uri Saguy, a former Israeli military intelligence chief said: "About as much as aspirin has on flu -- it is marginal and brings the fever down a bit but it doesn't cure the ailment itself."
